blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-security-1 (API tokens are stored in clear in the database) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-security-2 (The Authorization header is logged at info level) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
The `api_tokens` table holds `user_id`, `token` and `created_at`; the
middleware looks a request's token up with `WHERE token = $1`. Storing the
token as given keeps the lookup a simple indexed equality.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Tokens are stored as given
findings.recommendation: Store only a hash of the token (SHA-256 of the 32 random bytes is enough for a high-entropy secret, no bcrypt needed), and look it up with `WHERE token_hash = $1` on the hash of the presented token: the lookup stays a single indexed equality, so the "lookup must be fast" argument does not require the clear value. As written, anyone who reads the `api_tokens` table — a database backup, a read replica, a support SQL console, a later injection — obtains working bearer credentials for every integration of every user, and since revocation is a Non-Goal they cannot be invalidated (CWE-312, CWE-522). Update tasks 1.1 and 1.2 to match.
findings.title: API tokens are stored in clear in the database

findings.evidence:
To diagnose integration problems, the middleware logs each request's
method, path and headers at `info` level, including `Authorization`, so
support can see which token an integration sent.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Every request is logged with its headers
findings.recommendation: Redact secret headers before logging: drop or mask `Authorization` and `Cookie` (the middleware already reads the session from `Cookie`), and log instead a non-secret token identifier (a token id or a short prefix of the token's hash) so support can still tell which token an integration sent. As written, every bearer token and every session cookie lands in the logs: anyone with access to the log pipeline or a log export replays them and acts as the user, with no revocation to stop it (CWE-532). Update task 1.3 so `logs_requests` asserts the secret headers are absent.
findings.title: The Authorization header is logged at info level

findings.evidence: - [A user loses a token] → they create another one; revoking the old one comes with the later revocation change.
findings.recommendation: The proposal's motivation is that "a leaked integration exposes the account", yet with revocation deferred and no expiry a leaked token keeps working forever: an attacker holding it keeps full API access to the account and the user has no way to cut it off — creating another token does not disable the old one. Either ship a minimal revocation (delete the token's row) in this change, or give tokens an expiry until the revocation change lands, and state the residual risk in the design.
findings.title: A leaked token cannot be invalidated
